title.en: King and Queen of the Vaudoux: Moreau de Saint-Méry's Account
title.zh: 伏都之王與后：聖梅里的記述

region.zh: 法屬聖多明各（今海地）西部

texts.period: Recorded c. 1790 (Moreau de Saint-Méry); republished by St. John 1884

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V, reproducing Moreau de Saint-Méry's description of the Vaudoux (1790s)

summary.en: According to the Arada negroes, the true sectaries of the Vaudoux, the word signifies an all-powerful and supernatural being on whom depend all the events which take place in the world: the non-venomous serpent, through whose grand priest and high priestess — the King and Queen, or Master and Mistress, or the touching titles of Papa and Mama — all its knowledge of the past, the present and the future is communicated. The two delegates, chiefs for life of the great family of the Vaudoux, keep the serpent in its box upon the altar; petitioners bring their vows of eternal love or maledictions against a rival; the Queen, mounted on the sacred ark, is seized by the spirit and the oracle speaks by her mouth; and the offerings gathered in a covered hat pay the expenses of the meetings and give aid to absent or needy members — a secret society that functioned, in part, as a burial-and-relief fund.
summary.zh: 據真正的伏都教眾阿爾達黑人所言：『伏都』意即一位全能超凡之存在——無毒之蛇——世上諸事皆繫於它；其神諭只借大祭司與女大祭司之口而傳——人稱王與后、主與母、或親暱的爸爸媽媽。二位終身執掌伏都大家族，蛇靈伏於祭壇木匣之中；祈願者帶來永恆之愛的誓詞或詛咒情敵的惡語；王后立於神匣之上，神靈附體，神諭借其口而出；以蓋帽收下的獻金支付聚會開支，並接濟遠行或困乏的會友——這個秘密結社，實亦兼作互助與喪葬金會。

sensitivity.note: 18th-century colonial description (Moreau de Saint-Méry) reproduced through St. John's late-19th-century hostile framing. The society's relief-fund function is in the source text itself; the record preserves the balance between the source's sensationalism and its documentary detail. Living religion: liturgy not reproduced.

passages.text: According to the Arada negroes, who are the true sectaries of the Vaudoux in the colony, and maintain its principles and its rules, Vaudoux signifies an all-powerful and supernatural being, on whom depend all the events which take place in the world. This being is the non-venomous serpent, and it is under its auspices that all those assemble who profess this doctrine. Acquaintance with the past, knowledge of the present, prescience of the future, all appertain to this serpent, that only consents to communicate his power and prescribe his will through the organ of a grand priest, whom the sectaries select, and still more by that of the negress whom the love of the latter has raised to the rank of high priestess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V, reproducing Moreau de Saint-Méry (1884/1790s); not verbatim.

passages.text: These two delegates, who declare themselves inspired by their god — or in whom the gift of inspiration is really manifested in the opinion of their followers — bear the pompous names of King and Queen, or the despotic ones of Master and Mistress, or the touching titles of Papa and Mama. They are during their whole life the chiefs of the great family of the Vaudoux, and they have a right to the unlimited respect of the sectaries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: A young one solicits eternal love, or she repeats the maledictions that hate dictates against a preferred rival; there is not a passion which does not give vent to its vow. At each of these invocations the King of the Vaudoux appears absorbed in thought; the spirit seizes him, and suddenly he takes hold of the box in which the serpent is confined, places it on the ground, and commands the Queen to get on it. As soon as the sacred ark is beneath her feet, the new Pythoness is filled by the spirit of their god; she trembles, all her body is in a state of convulsion, and the oracle speaks by her mouth — now she flatters and promises happiness, now she bursts into reproaches, dictating as decrees without appeal everything she is pleased to prescribe in the name of the serpent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: After the questions have received their answers, they form a circle and the serpent is again placed on the altar; his followers bring as tribute the objects they think most worthy, and that no jealous curiosity may raise a blush the offerings are placed in a covered hat. The King and Queen promise the offerings shall be accepted by their god. It is from this collection that the expenses of the meetings are paid, that aid is afforded to absent members, or to those present who may be in want, or to others from whom the society may expect something in favor of its glory or renown — and a fresh oath engages each one to be silent as to what has passed, sometimes sealed by the warm blood of a goat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The Initiation Circle and the Monter-Vaudou in Old Saint-Domingue
title.zh: 聖多明各的入會圈與『上伏都』

region.zh: 法屬聖多明各（今海地）西部

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V — the dance of the Vaudoux and the admission of new candidates

summary.en: The fete begins with the admission of the candidate: the King traces a large circle with some black substance and places the novice within it, a packet of herbs, horsehair, pieces of horn and other trifling objects in his hand; lightly touching his head with a wooden wand, he thunders forth an African song repeated in chorus around the circle — then the new member begins to tremble and to dance, which is called to practise Vaudoux. If excess of excitement makes him leave the circle the song stops, the King and Queen turn their backs to avert the evil omen; he re-enters, trembles, drinks, and arrives at so convulsive a state that the King stops him with a touch of the wand — and from that moment he belongs to the sect.
summary.zh: 慶典以收徒開場：王以黑物畫一大圈，置新會者於圈中，手捧藥草、馬鬃、獸角諸物；木杖輕點其頂，朗聲唱起非洲古調，圈眾應聲而和——於是新會者顫慄起舞，是謂『行伏都』。若狂喜過度而跨出圈外，歌聲立止，王與后背身轉向以避凶兆；其人回圈再顫、復飲，終至痙攣之境，王以杖點其頂止之——自那一刻起，他便屬於這個教團。

sensitivity.note: 18th-century colonial description; the same ceremony reappears in the 1904 Cuban record (cross_ref: afroatlantic-louisiana-voodoo-rites, afroatlantic-vaudoux-king-queen). Living religion: initiation liturgy not reproduced.

passages.text: After these ceremonies commences the dance of the Vaudoux. If there should be a new candidate, it is by his admission that the fete commences. The King of the Vaudoux, with some black substance, traces a large circle, and in this the novice is placed; and in his hand he puts a packet of herbs, horsehair, pieces of horn, and other trifling objects.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V (1884/1790s); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then lightly touching him on the head with a slight wooden wand, he thunders forth an African song, which is repeated in chorus by those who stand around the circle; then the new member begins to tremble and to dance, which is called to practise Vaudoux. If, unhappily, excess of excitement makes him leave the circle, the song immediately ceases, the King and Queen turn their backs to avert the evil omen. The dancer recollects himself, re-enters the circle, again trembles, drinks, and arrives at length at so convulsive a state that the King orders him to stop by striking him lightly on the head with his wand. He is taken to the altar to swear, and from that moment he belongs to the sect.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: This ceremony over, the King places his hand or his foot on the box in which the serpent is confined, and soon becomes agitated; this impression he communicates to the Queen, and from her it gains the whole circle, and every one commences certain movements in which the upper part of the body, the head and shoulders, appear to be dislocated — a nervous trembling seizes them all, which they appear unable to master. In reading this account, freely given from Moreau de Saint-Méry, St. John was struck how little change, except for the worse, had taken place during the last century.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

title.en: The 1864 Trial and the Empty Graves
title.zh: 一八六四年審判與空墳之謎

texts.period: Historical event of 1864, described in a hostile colonial account (St. John, 1884)

source.work: Sir Spenser St. John, 'Hayti; or, The Black Republic' (1884), ch. V — the trial at which the author was present, and the disappearances after execution

summary.en: The eight convicts of the 1864 sorcery trial were executed in white robes on a market-day for solemnity — and the Vaudoux priests gave out that although the deity would permit the execution, he would only do it to prove his power by raising them all again from the dead. Piquets of troops were placed round the burial place to prevent the bodies being carried away in the night; but in the morning three of the graves were found empty — the bodies of the two priests and the priestess had disappeared; superstitious fear had probably unmanned the sentries, and as most of the troops belonged to the sect, they probably connived at rather than prevented the exhumation.
summary.zh: 一八六四年巫案八名死囚著白袍於集市之日處決——而伏都祭司放話：神雖允許行刑，卻要以此證其大能，將八人全數復活。當局以衛兵環守葬地防人夜掘；翌晨三座墳墓已空——兩位祭司與女祭司的遺體不翼而飛。或許是迷信之懼令哨兵不敢久留；而部隊多屬教團中人，與其說阻止了開棺，不如說暗中成全。

sensitivity.note: SENSITIVE: This record treats the 1864 Port-au-Prince 'Vaudoux' executions as historical event within a colonial-era source whose accusations of ritual murder were part of a polemic (St. John's chapter was widely republished as anti-Vodou propaganda). Modern scholarship reads these trial narratives skeptically as colonial sensationalism; the record preserves the documented elements (trial, executions, claim of resurrection, empty graves) without reproducing gore, and flags the source bias. This is not representative of Vodou, a living religion.

passages.text: The trial was held before a judge who conducted himself with dignity, and whose court heard testimony from a young girl witness — protected from the prisoners' intimidation by being placed with her back to them while she whispered her story to the judge — and from other witnesses, until the guilt of the prisoners was fully established. They were all found guilty of sorcery, torture, and murder, and condemned to death. The execution took place on Saturday, February 13, 1864, the authorities wisely selecting a market-day in order that the example might have the greater effect; the prisoners, men and women, were all clothed in white robes and white headdresses — the garments reserved for parricides — and were drawn in carts to the place of execution.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, Hayti, ch. V (1884); details of the alleged crimes deliberately summarized without gore; not verbatim.

passages.text: The troops and National Guard were summoned, for even the word rescue had been pronounced; the prisoners, tied in pairs, were placed in a line and faced by five soldiers to each pair. As usual the prisoners behaved with great courage, even the women standing up unflinchingly before their executioners.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Vaudoux priests gave out that although the deity would permit the execution, he would only do it to prove to his votaries his power by raising them all again from the dead. To prevent their bodies being carried away during the night — they had been buried near the place of execution — piquets of troops were placed round the spot; but in the morning three of the graves were found empty, and the bodies of the two priests and the priestess had disappeared. Superstitious fear had probably prevented the soldiers from staying where they had been posted, and as most of the troops belonged to the sect of the Vaudoux, they probably connived at, rather than prevented, the exhumation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of St. John, ch. V (1884); not verbatim.
